claim: Neurons in primate visual cortex encode which object owns a border (border ownership).
source: Neurons in primate visual cortex encode which object owns a border (border ownership), but the underlying circuitry is not understood.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited in the abstract as background for the study.

claim: Border ownership selectivity occurs first in deep layer units in V4.
source: We find that border ownership selectivity occurs first in deep layer units, in contrast to spike latency for small stimuli in the classical receptive field.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Units on the same penetration typically share the preferred side of border ownership, also across layers.
source: Units on the same penetration typically share the preferred side of border ownership, also across layers, similar to orientation preference.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Units are often border ownership-selective for a range of border orientations.
source: Units are often border ownership-selective for a range of border orientations, where the preferred sides of border ownership are systematically organized in visual space.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The earliest border ownership signals in V4 are not simply inherited from upstream areas.
source: Together our data reveal a columnar organization of border ownership in V4 where the earliest border ownership signals are not simply inherited from upstream areas, but computed by neurons in deep layers
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding laminar timing differences.

claim: Border ownership signals computed in deep layers may be part of signals fed back to upstream cortical areas or the oculomotor system early after stimulus onset.
source: and may thus be part of signals fed back to upstream cortical areas or the oculomotor system early after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the timing and laminar location of border ownership signals.

claim: The asymmetric context integrated by border ownership neurons is provided in a systematically clustered manner, possibly through corticocortical feedback and horizontal connections.
source: The finding that preferred border ownership is clustered and can cover a wide range of spatially contiguous locations suggests that the asymmetric context integrated by these neurons is provided in a systematically clustered manner, possibly through corticocortical feedback and horizontal connections.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering findings with speculation about underlying mechanisms.

claim: Border ownership represents a fundamental computation in visual perception that is thought to be critical to visual scene segmentation and object recognition.
source: Border ownership represents a fundamental computation in visual perception that is thought to be critical to visual scene segmentation and object recognition (Nakayama et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Von der Heydt et al. discovered neurons in primate visual cortex that are selective for border ownership, most prominently in extrastriate visual areas V2 and V4.
source: Von der Heydt et al. discovered neurons in primate visual cortex that are selective for border ownership, most prominently in extrastriate visual areas V2 and V4 (Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a historical fact about the discovery of border ownership neurons, supported by citation.

claim: Feedforward inputs arrive primarily in the granular (input) layer.
source: These pathways have a distinct laminar organization: feedforward inputs arrive primarily in the granular (input) layer, whereas horizontal and corticocortical feedback connections predominantly target superficial and deep layers (Douglas and Martin, 2004; Rockland and Pandya, 1979; Rockland et al., 1994; Rockland and Lund, 1983; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986; Yoshioka et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical anatomy, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Horizontal and corticocortical feedback connections predominantly target superficial and deep layers.
source: These pathways have a distinct laminar organization: feedforward inputs arrive primarily in the granular (input) layer, whereas horizontal and corticocortical feedback connections predominantly target superficial and deep layers (Douglas and Martin, 2004; Rockland and Pandya, 1979; Rockland et al., 1994; Rockland and Lund, 1983; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986; Yoshioka et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical anatomy, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Primate areas V1 and V2 contain orientation columns.
source: Primate areas V1 and V2 contain orientation columns (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987; Hubel et al., 1978; Vanduffel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical organization, supported by citations.

claim: Imaging studies indicate that there is at least clustering of orientation preference in superficial layers of V4.
source: In V4, imaging studies indicate that there is at least clustering of orientation preference in superficial layers of V4 (Ghose and Ts'o, 1997; Roe et al., 2012; Tanigawa et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from imaging studies, supported by citations.

claim: It is unclear whether orientation clusters in V4 are columnar.
source: In V4, imaging studies indicate that there is at least clustering of orientation preference in superficial layers of V4 (Ghose and Ts'o, 1997; Roe et al., 2012; Tanigawa et al., 2010), although it is unclear whether these clusters are columnar.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: Prior studies have focused on orientation-selective units and tested border ownership at the neuron's preferred orientation, without examining the relationship between orientation preference and border ownership preference.
source: Prior studies have focused on orientation-selective units and tested border ownership at the neuron's preferred orientation, without examining the relationship between orientation preference and border ownership preference (Hesse and Tsao, 2016; Zhang and von der Heydt, 2010; Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Data were obtained from two rhesus macaques recorded over 88 penetrations.
source: We present data from two rhesus macaques recorded over 88 penetrations (animal Z: 34; animal D: 54).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental dataset.

claim: Laminar analyses are performed for 81 penetrations for which the current source density (CSD) analysis was interpretable.
source: Laminar analyses are performed for 81 penetrations for which the current source density (CSD) analysis (see below and Methods) was interpretable.
evidence: This describes the subset of data used for laminar analysis.

claim: The orthogonal position of the probe relative to the cortical surface resulted in a vertical stacking of the RFs from different electrode contacts.
source: The orthogonal position of the probe relative to the cortical surface resulted in a vertical stacking of the RFs from different electrode contacts (Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental setup, supported by figures.

claim: The median distance between RF centers per mm depth along the probe was 0.83°/mm with an interquartile range of 1.00°/mm for 81 penetrations.
source: Orthogonality was evaluated by computing the distance between RF centers per mm depth along the probe (D in Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Methods; median [interquartile range] 0.83°/mm [1.00°/mm], n = 81 penetrations).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: 685 well-isolated units were included in the analysis.
source: This resulted in 685 well-isolated units (animal Z: 227; animal D: 458) and 765 multiunit clusters (animal Z: 329; animal D: 436).
evidence: This describes the number of units analyzed in the study.

claim: 765 multiunit clusters were included in the analysis.
source: This resulted in 685 well-isolated units (animal Z: 227; animal D: 458) and 765 multiunit clusters (animal Z: 329; animal D: 436).
evidence: This describes the number of multiunit clusters analyzed in the study.

claim: The unit shown in Figure 1B has a border ownership index of 0.38 with p < 0.0001.
source: We assessed statistical significance of border ownership selectivity with a permutation test on the absolute value of the border ownership index (BOI, see Methods, |BOI| = 0.38 for this unit, permutation test p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result for an example unit.

claim: CSD analysis results in a pattern of current sinks and current sources.
source: This analysis results in a pattern of current sinks and current sources (Figure 1F shows an example CSD map for the penetration during which the unit in Figure 1B was recorded).
evidence: This describes the output of the CSD analysis method.

claim: CSD maps show a prominent leading current sink in the central portion of the penetration.
source: Such maps show a prominent leading current sink in the central portion of the penetration (white star in Figure 1F), with a current source followed by a current sink on the electrode contacts positioned deep from it (white disc in Figure 1F).
evidence: This describes a consistent pattern observed in CSD maps.

claim: The sink-source pattern in CSD maps occurred consistently in different penetrations.
source: This sink–source pattern occurred consistently in different penetrations (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of the CSD pattern across recordings.

claim: Studies from other laboratories in behaving macaques have described the same sink-source pattern in area V4.
source: Studies from other laboratories in behaving macaques have described this sink–source pattern as well in area V4 (Pettine et al., 2019, their Figure 1C; Lu et al., 2018, their Figure S4B)
evidence: This cites corroborating evidence from other studies.

claim: Takeuchi et al. found that the prominent early current sink indicates the position of the granular layer through histological verification.
source: Takeuchi et al. paired this analysis with histological verification by applying electrolytic marks during the recordings and found that the prominent early current sink indicates the position of the granular layer (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), thus consistent with CSD analysis in V1 (Mitzdorf, 1985).
evidence: This cites histological validation from another study.

claim: 51.1% of well-isolated units show border ownership selectivity.
source: Across the population, we find border ownership selectivity in 51.1% of well-isolated units (350 out of 685 units
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the population analysis.

claim: 44.6% of units show border ownership selectivity when pooling across well-isolated and multiunit clusters.
source: pooling across well-isolated and multiunit clusters, we find border ownership selectivity in 44.6% of units [647 out of 1450 units]
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the combined population analysis.

claim: The proportion of border ownership-selective units is high in all laminar compartments.
source: This proportion is high in all laminar compartments (superficial: 43.3% [58 out of 134]; granular: 57.3% [102 out of 178]; deep: 56.0% [121 out of 216]; pooled well-isolated and multiunit clusters: superficial: 42.8% [140 out of 327]; granular: 51.5% [167 out of 324]; deep: 49.1% [210 out of 428]).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing the distribution across layers.

claim: Border ownership selectivity occurs early after onset of the stimulus-evoked response.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Zhou et al., 2000), we observe that border ownership selectivity (difference in response to the preferred and the non-preferred side) occurs early after onset of the stimulus-evoked response.
evidence: This is an observation from the time course analysis, consistent with prior work.

claim: The difference between responses to preferred and non-preferred sides of border ownership first becomes statistically significant at 56.5 ms after stimulus onset for all border ownership-selective well-isolated units.
source: The asterisk indicates when the difference between these functions first becomes statistically significant (56.5 ms after stimulus onset; sign rank test p < 0.05 for 20 adjacent ms).
evidence: This is a specific timing measurement from the population analysis.

claim: In superficial layers, the difference between responses to preferred and non-preferred sides becomes significant at 85.8 ms.
source: When evaluating these functions in each laminar compartment we observe that these functions diverge substantially early after onset in deep cortical layers (Figure 2D; significant at 58.8 ms), but later in superficial (Figure 2B; significant at 85.8 ms) and granular layers (Figure 2C; significant at 67.3 ms).
evidence: This is a specific timing measurement for superficial layers.

claim: In granular layers, the difference between responses to preferred and non-preferred sides becomes significant at 67.3 ms.
source: When evaluating these functions in each laminar compartment we observe that these functions diverge substantially early after onset in deep cortical layers (Figure 2D; significant at 58.8 ms), but later in superficial (Figure 2B; significant at 85.8 ms) and granular layers (Figure 2C; significant at 67.3 ms).
evidence: This is a specific timing measurement for granular layers.

claim: In deep layers, the difference between responses to preferred and non-preferred sides becomes significant at 58.8 ms.
source: When evaluating these functions in each laminar compartment we observe that these functions diverge substantially early after onset in deep cortical layers (Figure 2D; significant at 58.8 ms), but later in superficial (Figure 2B; significant at 85.8 ms) and granular layers (Figure 2C; significant at 67.3 ms).
evidence: This is a specific timing measurement for deep layers.

claim: Differences in sample size between layers do not explain the shorter latency for deep layers.
source: This definition of latency depends on sample size, but a subsampling analysis shows that differences in sample size between layers do not explain the shorter latency for deep layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a control analysis to rule out a confounding factor.

claim: Border ownership latency was significantly shorter for deep layer units (75.8 ms, 95% CI [68.4 85.2]) than for granular layer units (94.7 ms, 95% CI [82.2 105.7], bootstrap procedure p = 0.006).
source: Latency was significantly shorter for deep layer units (75.8 ms, 95% CI [68.4 85.2]) than for granular layer units (94.7 ms, 95% CI [82.2 105.7], bootstrap procedure [see Methods] p = 0.006)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of latencies between layers.

claim: Border ownership latency was significantly shorter for deep layer units (75.8 ms, 95% CI [68.4 85.2]) than for superficial layer units (97.7 ms, 95% CI [78.0 103.7], bootstrap procedure p = 0.018).
source: Latency was significantly shorter for deep layer units (75.8 ms, 95% CI [68.4 85.2]) than for granular layer units (94.7 ms, 95% CI [82.2 105.7], bootstrap procedure [see Methods] p = 0.006) and for superficial layer units (97.7 ms, 95% CI [78.0 103.7], bootstrap procedure p = 0.018).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of latencies between layers.

claim: When well-isolated units and multiunits were pooled, border ownership latency was significantly shorter for deep layers (78.2 ms) than for granular layers (94.0 ms, p = 0.007) and superficial layers (100.7 ms, p = 0.009).
source: The same was true when well-isolated units and multiunits were pooled (deep: 78.2 ms, 95% CI [73.3 88.2], n = 210; granular: 94.0 ms, 95% CI [87.9 106.5], n = 167; superficial: 100.7 ms, 95% CI [85.1 104.6], n = 140; deep vs. granular: p = 0.007; deep vs. superficial: p = 0.009).
evidence: This confirms the latency difference with a larger dataset.

claim: Border ownership reliability (BOR) rises earlier in the deep layers (89.9 ms, 95% CI [81.5 99.9]) than in the granular (105.4 ms, 95% CI [94.9 114.6]; bootstrap procedure p = 0.015) and superficial layers (109.4, 95% CI [98.9 124.9]; p = 0.006).
source: Again we find that BOR rises earlier in the deep layers (89.9 ms, 95% CI [81.5 99.9]) than in the granular (105.4 ms, 95% CI [94.9 114.6]; bootstrap procedure p = 0.015) and superficial layers (109.4, 95% CI [98.9 124.9]; p = 0.006).
evidence: This is an alternative analysis confirming the timing differences between layers.

claim: After border ownership selectivity has been established, the average border ownership index tends to be higher in the deep compartment (0.50 ± 0.02) than in the granular (0.43 ± 0.02) and superficial compartment (0.45 ± 0.03), but the differences do not reach statistical significance.
source: After border ownership selectivity has been established, the average border ownership index tends to be higher in the deep compartment (Figure 2E; BOI between 200 and 500 ms after stimulus onset: mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], 0.50 ± 0.02) than in the granular (0.43 ± 0.02) and superficial compartment (0.45 ± 0.03), but the differences do not reach statistical significance (deep vs. granular: Wilcoxon rank sum test p = 0.051; deep vs. superficial: p = 0.22).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of border ownership strength across layers.

claim: BOR saturates around 0.85 in all three compartments.
source: BOR saturates around 0.85 in all three compartments (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an observation about the maximum reliability across layers.

claim: Border ownership selectivity does not occur first in granular layer units but instead in deep layer units.
source: Together, these data indicate that border ownership selectivity does not occur first in granular layer units but instead in deep layer units.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the timing analyses.

claim: For responses to small ring stimuli in the cRF, the latency is shorter in the granular layer compared to the deep layers and superficial layers.
source: First, we evaluated the latency of spikes evoked by small ring stimuli in the cRF. For these responses we find, in contrast to border ownership selectivity, that the latency is shorter in the granular layer compared to the deep layers and superficial layers (Figure 3; latency defined as crossing of the functions with a threshold value a third of the way from baseline to peak).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing different laminar timing for a different type of response.

claim: For contrast polarity index functions, there is no earlier rise in selectivity in the deep layers.
source: Second, we evaluated the responses to the border ownership stimuli for another type of selectivity, contrast polarity. This refers to the relative luminance contrast across the edge, that is the difference between panels 1 and 3 (or between panels 2 and 4) in Figure 1A. For the contrast polarity index functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), we do not find an earlier rise in selectivity in the deep layers, even though they are derived from the same units as in Figure 2.
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that early deep layer selectivity is specific to border ownership.

claim: The earlier selectivity in deep layers compared to granular and superficial layers is specific for border ownership.
source: Together, these data indicate that the earlier selectivity in deep layers compared to granular and superficial layers is specific for border ownership.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control analyses.

claim: For a given edge, the two possible sides of border ownership are encoded by distinct subpopulations of neurons that are similar in size.
source: Our data show indeed that these two subpopulations exist in similar proportions (Figure 4A, top). The same is true for units that encode border ownership for horizontal edges (Figure 4A, bottom), and when we express the preferred side of border ownership not relative to the screen, but relative to the fixation point (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This indicates that for a given edge, the two possible sides of border ownership are encoded by distinct subpopulations of neurons that are similar in size.
evidence: This is a finding about the population organization of border ownership preferences.

claim: In the population of all penetrations with at least four border ownership units, the proportion of units that share the same preferred side of border ownership is significantly higher than chance (well-isolated units: 74.4%, randomization test p = 0.017).
source: In the population of all penetrations with at least four border ownership units, the proportion of units that share the same preferred side of border ownership is significantly higher than chance (well-isolated units: 74.4%, randomization test p = 0.017, 23 penetrations with 110 units
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing clustering of border ownership preference.

claim: Including multiunit clusters, 71.7% of units share the same preferred side of border ownership (p = 0.005, 47 penetrations with 288 units).
source: including multiunit clusters: 71.7%, p = 0.005, 47 penetrations with 288 units
evidence: This confirms the clustering finding with a larger dataset.

claim: In penetrations with border ownership units spanning from superficial to deep layers, there is significant clustering of border ownership preference (well-isolated units: 81.1%, randomization test p = 0.010).
source: Also in the subgroup of penetrations with border ownership units spanning from superficial to deep layers, we find significant clustering (Figure 4D; well-isolated units: 81.1%, randomization test p = 0.010, 6 penetrations with 30 units
evidence: This shows that clustering extends across layers.

claim: Including multiunit clusters, 73.7% of units spanning layers share the same preferred side of border ownership (p = 0.003, 20 penetrations with 136 units).
source: including multiunit clusters: 73.7%, p = 0.003, 20 penetrations with 136 units
evidence: This confirms the cross-layer clustering with a larger dataset.

claim: Border ownership preference is organized in spatial clusters that span cortical layers in a columnar fashion.
source: Together, these data indicate that border ownership preference is organized in spatial clusters that span cortical layers in a columnar fashion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the clustering analyses.

claim: Several imaging studies have shown that preferred orientation is spatially clustered in V4 in domains.
source: Similar to our finding that preferred border ownership is clustered, several imaging studies have shown that preferred orientation is spatially clustered in V4 in domains (e.g., Li et al., 2013; Tanigawa et al., 2010)
evidence: This cites prior imaging studies on orientation clustering.

claim: It is not known whether orientation clusters in V4 form columns.
source: Similar to our finding that preferred border ownership is clustered, several imaging studies have shown that preferred orientation is spatially clustered in V4 in domains (e.g., Li et al., 2013; Tanigawa et al., 2010), but it is not known whether these form columns.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Orientation preference in V4 is shared in clusters that extend vertically across layers.
source: To test whether orientation preference in V4 is shared in clusters that extend vertically across layers, we determined orientation tuning for the units in our sample from responses to luminance contrast edges centered on the cRF (independent data set from the border ownership stimuli, see Methods). Our data confirm clustering of preferred orientation and reveal that these clusters span across laminar compartments in V4 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the orientation tuning analysis.

claim: For 9 out of 18 penetrations with at least four orientation-selective well-isolated units distributed over all three laminar compartments, the aggregate preferred orientation was statistically significant (p < 0.05).
source: For each of these six penetrations, this resultant was significantly larger than expected from the null distribution (p < 0.05). This was true for 9 out of 18 penetrations with at least four orientation-selective well-isolated units distributed over all three laminar compartments
evidence: This is a statistical finding about orientation clustering across layers.

claim: For 17 out of 34 penetrations when well-isolated units and multiunit clusters were pooled, the aggregate preferred orientation was statistically significant.
source: (for 17 out of 34 penetrations when well-isolated units and multiunit clusters were pooled).
evidence: This confirms the orientation clustering finding with a larger dataset.

claim: Orientation domains in V4 are columnar.
source: These data suggest that orientation domains in V4 are columnar.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the orientation clustering analysis.

claim: Border ownership selectivity is significantly more common in units that are selective for orientation (53.3%) than in those that are not (36.8%, Chi square = 9.51, p = 0.002).
source: We find that border ownership selectivity is significantly more common in units that are selective for orientation than in those that are not, but it is also surprisingly common in units that are not selective for orientation (Table 1, respectively, 53.3% and 36.8%, Chi square = 9.51, p = 0.002
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between orientation and border ownership selectivity.

claim: Including multiunit clusters, border ownership selectivity is significantly more common in orientation-selective units (45.9%) than in non-orientation-selective units (31.3%, Chi square = 19.5, p = 0.00001).
source: including multiunit clusters: respectively, 45.9% and 31.3%, Chi square = 19.5, p = 0.00001
evidence: This confirms the relationship with a larger dataset.

claim: The average orientation of edges with border ownership selectivity is mildly biased toward the preferred orientation for edges.
source: At the population level, the average orientation of edges with border ownership selectivity is indeed mildly biased toward the preferred orientation for edges. This is subtle but can be seen as the tendency of the data points in Figure 6C to appear close to the identity lines.
evidence: This is an observation from the population analysis of orientation and border ownership.

claim: The average distance of edge orientations with border ownership selectivity to the preferred orientation is 27.6°, significantly smaller than chance (randomization test p = 0.018; n = 68 well-isolated units).
source: This distance is on average distance 27.6°, significantly smaller than chance (randomization test [see Materials and methods] p = 0.018; n = 68 well-isolated units tested with at least four orientations
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the relationship between border ownership and orientation preference.

claim: Including multiunit clusters, the bias toward preferred orientation is significant (p = 0.017; n = 159).
source: including multiunit clusters: p = 0.017; n = 159
evidence: This confirms the bias with a larger dataset.

claim: Orientation-tuned units tend to be border ownership-selective for edges with an orientation near their preferred orientation, but this relation is surprisingly subtle.
source: Orientation-tuned units thus tend to be border ownership-selective for edges with an orientation near their preferred orientation, but this relation is surprisingly subtle.
evidence: This is a summary of the relationship between orientation and border ownership preferences.

claim: 29.7% of border ownership-selective well-isolated units (n = 182) show border ownership selectivity to edges that maximally differ in orientation (orthogonal edges).
source: Furthermore, we find that border ownership-selective units often show border ownership selectivity to edges that maximally differ in orientation, that is orthogonal edges. An example unit is shown in the right panel in Figure 6A (cyan triangle). This is true for 29.7 % of border ownership-selective well-isolated units (n = 182
evidence: This is a finding about the breadth of border ownership tuning.

claim: 24.4% of border ownership-selective units including multiunits (n = 353) show border ownership selectivity to orthogonal edges.
source: 24.4 % including multiunits, n = 353
evidence: This confirms the finding with a larger dataset.

claim: For all 24 out of 24 well-isolated units that were selective for the border ownership of squares at orthogonal and intermediate orientations, the preferred side of border ownership for intermediate orientations was spatially contiguous.
source: We find that for all 24 out of 24 well-isolated units that were selective for the border ownership of squares at orthogonal and intermediate orientations, the preferred side of border ownership for these intermediate orientations was spatially contiguous (such as the example in Figure 6B, right panel
evidence: This is a finding about the spatial organization of border ownership preferences.

claim: Including multiunits, for 35 out of 35 units selective for border ownership at orthogonal and intermediate orientations, the preferred sides were spatially contiguous.
source: including multiunits, this is true for 35 out of 35 units
evidence: This confirms the spatial contiguity finding with a larger dataset.

claim: 18.0% of border ownership units have an area of preferred sides of border ownership that spans at least 120°.
source: A span of at least this width occurs for 18.0 % of border ownership units (Figure 6E
evidence: This is a finding about the breadth of border ownership preferences in visual space.

claim: 15.4% of border ownership units including multiunit clusters have an area of preferred sides spanning at least 120°.
source: 15.4 % including multiunit clusters
evidence: This confirms the finding with a larger dataset.

claim: About half of the neurons responsive to edges in V2 are selective for border ownership.
source: Given that about half of the neurons responsive to edges in V2 are selective for border ownership (Zhou et al., 2000), neurons in V4 could simply inherit this property from V2 through the feedforward projection from V2 to V4.
evidence: This cites a prior finding about border ownership in V2.

claim: The feedforward projection from V2 to V4 is the most important source of feedforward input to V4.
source: This projection is the most important source of feedforward input to V4 (Markov et al., 2011)
evidence: This cites anatomical knowledge about V4 inputs.

claim: The V2 to V4 projection targets mostly layer 4 (granular layer) in V4.
source: and targets mostly layer 4 (granular layer) in V4 (Gattass et al., 1997; Rockland, 1992).
evidence: This cites anatomical knowledge about the laminar target of V2-V4 projections.

claim: Spike latency for stimuli in the cRF is shortest in the granular layer, similar to what has been described in other areas in macaque visual cortex.
source: Our data show that spike latency for stimuli in the cRF is shortest in the granular layer, which is similar to what has been described in other areas in macaque visual cortex (V1: e.g., Nowak et al., 1995; MT: Raiguel et al., 1999), and consistent with work by others in awake V4 (Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior work in other cortical areas.

claim: In anesthetized V2, spike latency has been reported to be longer in layer 4 than in infragranular layers.
source: Note that this may not be universal across areas: in anesthetized V2 spike latency has been reported to be longer in layer 4 than in infragranular layers (Nowak et al., 1995).
evidence: This cites an exception to the general pattern in a different area.

claim: Deep layer neurons receive significant input from nearly all cortical layers, regardless of cell type, as opposed to neurons in other layers.
source: Scanning laser photostimulation studies in primary visual cortex showed that layer 5 neurons receive significant input from nearly all cortical layers, regardless of cell type, as opposed to neurons in other layers (Briggs and Callaway, 2005; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites anatomical findings about deep layer connectivity.

claim: Deep layers of the cortex include tall pyramidal cells whose apical dendrites reach up to layer 1.
source: Deep layers of the cortex, including in primates, include tall pyramidal cells whose apical dendrites reach up to layer 1, which could thus directly sample and integrate afferent information that arrives in a wide range of layers (Binzegger et al., 2004; Callaway, 1998; Lund and Boothe, 1975; Markov et al., 2014; Zarrinpar and Callaway, 2016).
evidence: This cites anatomical knowledge about deep layer neuron morphology.

claim: Corticocortical feedback in V4 terminates densely in all layers except layer 4.
source: Corticocortical feedback in V4 terminates densely in all layers except layer 4 (Markov et al., 2011; Rockland et al., 1994).
evidence: This cites anatomical knowledge about feedback projections to V4.

claim: Intra-areal horizontal connections are prominent in layer 2/3 and in layer 5.
source: Intra-areal horizontal connections are prominent in layer 2/3 and in layer 5 (Lund et al., 1993; Yoshioka et al., 1992; Douglas and Martin, 2007).
evidence: This cites anatomical knowledge about horizontal connections.

claim: Studies in V2 showed that border ownership selectivity does not rely on a small number of localized object features but instead occurs through integration of extraclassical stimulus features over large areas of visual space.
source: Indeed, studies in V2 showed that border ownership selectivity does not rely on a small number of localized object features but instead occurs through integration of extraclassical stimulus features over large areas of visual space (Zhang and von der Heydt, 2010).
evidence: This cites prior findings about the spatial extent of border ownership computation.

claim: Calcium spikes in apical dendrites of layer five neurons can amplify the effects of feedback inputs.
source: Specialized intrinsic properties could further assist in this integration, such as the calcium spikes in apical dendrites of layer five neurons that can amplify the effects of feedback inputs (Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites a mechanism that could support integration in deep layer neurons.

claim: V4 is the dominant source of cortical feedback to V2.
source: First, V4 is the dominant source of cortical feedback to V2
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about cortical connectivity.

claim: 75% of feedback neurons from V4 to V2 are located in deep layers in V4.
source: and 75 % of these feedback neurons are located in deep layers in V4 (Markov et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites anatomical data about the laminar origin of feedback projections.

claim: V4 deep layers include neurons that project to the superior colliculus.
source: Second, V4 deep layers include neurons that project to the superior colliculus (Fries, 1984; Gattass et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites anatomical knowledge about V4 projections to subcortical structures.

claim: Saccades target objects more frequently than background.
source: Saccades target objects more frequently than background (Rothkopf et al., 2007).
evidence: This cites a behavioral finding about saccade targeting.

claim: Border ownership signals are established in deep layers well before 100 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Our data show that these signals are established in deep layers well before 100 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a summary of the timing findings.

claim: The intersaccadic interval is typically on the order of 200-300 ms.
source: They are thus computed quickly enough to allow time for saccade planning within the intersaccadic interval, which is typically on the order of 200–300 ms (Otero-Millan et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites a behavioral measurement about saccade timing.

claim: Deep layer V4 neurons encode more information about the direction of planned eye movements than do superficial neurons.
source: This proposed early role for deep layer neurons in supporting saccadic decisions is consistent with recent findings showing that deep layer V4 neurons encode more information about the direction of planned eye movements than do superficial neurons (Pettine et al., 2019).
evidence: This cites a recent finding that supports the proposed functional role.

claim: Prior studies on border ownership only evaluated border ownership selectivity at the preferred orientation of each neuron.
source: Prior studies on border ownership only evaluated border ownership selectivity at the preferred orientation of each neuron (Hesse and Tsao, 2016; Zhang and von der Heydt, 2010; Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This characterizes the approach of prior studies.

claim: Functional clustering is a recurring theme in primate cortical visual areas.
source: Functional clustering is a recurring theme in primate cortical visual areas (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987)
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical organization.

claim: Functional clustering has been reported for several modalities in V4 including orientation, hue, direction of motion, spatial frequency, and curvature.
source: and has been reported for several modalities in V4 including orientation, hue, direction of motion, spatial frequency, and recently curvature (Hu et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2018; Roe et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2020; Tanigawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This cites multiple studies showing clustering of different features in V4.

claim: Border ownership preference is preserved across layers within a vertical penetration.
source: We find here that border ownership preference is preserved across layers within a vertical penetration, indicating that this modality is also organized in a columnar fashion.
evidence: This is a summary of the clustering findings.

claim: The border ownership of an edge is computed based on stimulus features falling outside the cRF.
source: Importantly though, border ownership is of a fundamentally different nature than these other modalities: the border ownership of an edge is computed based on stimulus features falling outside the cRF.
evidence: This is a conceptual point about the nature of border ownership computation.

claim: The columnar organization of border ownership indicates that there is a systematic asymmetric arrangement of the extraclassical contextual information.
source: Combined with our finding that early border ownership signals are computed by deep layer neurons rather than being passed on from upstream areas, this columnar organization has important implications for the functional anatomy. It indicates that there is a systematic asymmetric arrangement of the extraclassical contextual information, which, as argued above, may be provided through horizontal fibers and corticocortical feedback.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the columnar organization finding.

claim: The clustered architecture of preferred border ownership requires clusters of asymmetric contextual information in cortex, such that opposite polarities of contextual information occur in distinct and complementary clusters.
source: The clustered architecture of preferred border ownership therefore requires clusters of asymmetric contextual information in cortex, such that opposite polarities of contextual information occur in distinct and complementary clusters.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the clustering findings.

claim: The substrate of border ownership clusters consists of clustered asymmetries in the retinotopic information carried by afferents from horizontal fibers and cortical feedback.
source: The present data indicate that border ownership selectivity initially does not arrive through the feedforward pathway. They thus suggest that the substrate of these clusters consists of clustered asymmetries in the retinotopic information carried by afferents from horizontal fibers and cortical feedback.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the anatomical substrate of border ownership clustering.

claim: Two male rhesus macaques were used in this study, aged 13 years (animal Z) and 15 years (animal D).
source: We obtained recordings in two male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), age 13 years (animal Z) and age 15 years (animal D).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: Both animals had no prior experimental history.
source: Both animals had no prior experimental history and were housed in separate cages in a primate room with up to six animals of the same species.
evidence: This describes the experimental history of the subjects.

claim: The study was performed in accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
source: This study was performed in accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
evidence: This describes the ethical guidelines followed.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Salk Institute for Biological Studies (protocol 14-00014).
source: All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Salk Institute for Biological Studies (protocol 14-00014).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: In a first surgical session, a titanium recording chamber was installed in a craniotomy over the prelunate gyrus.
source: In brief, in a first surgical session a titanium recording chamber was installed in a craniotomy over the prelunate gyrus, according to stereotactic coordinates derived from anatomical MRI scans from each animal (left hemisphere in animal Z, right hemisphere in animal D).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: In a second surgical session, the dura mater within the chamber was removed and replaced with a silicone-based optically clear artificial dura.
source: In a second surgical session, the dura mater within the chamber was removed, and replaced with a silicone-based optically clear artificial dura, establishing an optical window over dorsal area V4.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for establishing the recording window.

claim: A linear multielectrode probe with 32 channels and 100 µm electrode pitch was used.
source: A linear multielectrode probe (32-channel single-shaft acute probes, 100 µm electrode pitch [ATLAS Neuroengineering, Leuven, Belgium]) was mounted on the chamber using a hydraulic microdrive on an adjustable x–y stage (MO-972A, Narashige, Japan).
evidence: This describes the recording equipment used.

claim: The probe was positioned orthogonally relative to the cortical surface under visual guidance.
source: The probe was then lowered through the artificial dura over the prelunate gyrus, positioned orthogonally relative to the cortical surface under visual guidance (Zeiss microscope).
evidence: This describes the probe positioning procedure.

claim: The probe was advanced until multiunit activity was visible on the deepest ~2600 µm of the probe.
source: While monitoring the voltage signals from the electrodes for multiunit activity, the probe was lowered to penetrate the cortical surface. The probe was advanced until multiunit activity was visible on the deepest ~2600 µm of the probe.
evidence: This describes the recording procedure.

claim: Neural signals were recorded extracellularly, filtered and saved using Intan hardware.
source: Neural signals were recorded extracellularly, filtered and saved using Intan hardware (RHD2132 amplifier chip and RHD2000 amplifier evaluation system, Intan Technologies LLC, Los Angeles, USA) controlled by a Windows computer.
evidence: This describes the recording equipment and procedure.

claim: Visual stimuli were presented using a LED projector back-projected on a rear-projection screen positioned at 52 cm from the animal's eyes.
source: Visual stimuli were presented using a LED projector, back-projected on a rear-projection screen that was positioned at a distance of 52 cm from the animal's eyes (PROPixx, VPixx Technologies, Saint-Bruno, Canada).
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation setup.

claim: The MonkeyLogic software package was used for stimulus presentation, behavioral control and recording of eye position.
source: The MonkeyLogic software package developed in MATLAB (https://www.brown.edu/Research/monkeylogic/; https://monkeylogic.nimh.nih.gov/; Hwang et al., 2019) was used for stimulus presentation, behavioral control and recording of eye position.
evidence: This describes the software used for experimental control.

claim: Eye position was continuously monitored with an infrared eye tracking system.
source: Eye position was continuously monitored with an infrared eye tracking system (ISCAN model ETL-200, Woburn, MA) and eye traces were saved using MonkeyLogic.
evidence: This describes the eye tracking procedure.

claim: Trials were aborted if eye position deviated from the fixation point by more than a threshold (typically 1 dva radius).
source: Trials were aborted if eye position deviated from the fixation point (threshold typically 1 dva radius).
evidence: This describes the behavioral control procedure.

claim: RF mapping stimuli consisted of static modified Gabors and dark gray rings.
source: Stimuli consisted of static modified Gabors, constructed using square-wave instead of sinusoidal gratings, and dark gray rings (80 % luminance contrast, diameter 2 dva, thickness 0.25 dva).
evidence: This describes the stimuli used for receptive field mapping.

claim: The stimuli were presented every 50 or 60 ms while the animal maintained fixation.
source: The stimuli were presented every 50 or 60 ms while the animal maintained fixation.
evidence: This describes the temporal parameters of stimulus presentation.

claim: Each stimulus appeared at a random location selected from a grid sized 25 × 25 dva with 1 dva spacing.
source: Each stimulus appeared at a random location selected from a grid sized 25 × 25 dva with 1 dva spacing centered at coordinates [7.5 dva; 7.5 dva] in the appropriate visual quadrant.
evidence: This describes the spatial parameters of stimulus presentation.

claim: The CSD was calculated as the second spatial derivative of the stimulus-triggered LFP.
source: The CSD was calculated as the second spatial derivative of the stimulus-triggered LFP (filtered between 3.3 and 88 Hz) and visualized as spatial maps after smoothing using bicubic (2D) interpolation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; MATLAB function interp2 with option cubic, the spatial dimension was interpolated at a resolution of 10 µm)
evidence: This describes the CSD analysis method.

claim: The laminar analysis did not critically depend on the particular method of smoothing used for CSD maps.
source: but the laminar analysis did not critically depend on this particular method of smoothing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes a robustness check for the analysis method.

claim: Seven penetrations where the CSD map could not be interpreted were excluded from the laminar analyses.
source: Seven penetrations where the CSD map could not be interpreted were excluded from the laminar analyses
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for the analysis.

claim: Units were required to be located ≤2 mm from the most superficial channel with multiunit activity to be included in laminar analyses.
source: and we also required that all units included in the laminar analyses were located ≤2 mm from the most superficial channel with multiunit activity, to minimize the risk of including white matter activity.
evidence: This describes an inclusion criterion to ensure cortical recordings.

claim: Multiunit activity was derived as the amplitude of the envelope from the signal on each electrode contact by band-pass filtering between 500 Hz and 5 kHz, rectifying, and then low-pass filtering at 200 Hz.
source: To obtain an estimate for these RF positions, for the population of neurons in the vicinity of each electrode contact, we derived multiunit activity as the amplitude of the envelope from the signal on each electrode contact, by band-pass filtering the recorded signal between 500 Hz and 5 kHz, rectifying it and then low-pass filtering it at 200 Hz (adopting the approach from Self et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the method for extracting multiunit activity.

claim: RF contours at z = 3 were computed on the z-scored root mean square level of the analog multiunit signal.
source: RF contours at z = 3 were then computed on the z-scored root mean square level of this analog signal, using the same procedure as for the spiking data (see Receptive field mapping).
evidence: This describes the method for computing receptive field contours.

claim: The RF center was defined as the centroid of the region defined by the RF contour.
source: For each contour, the RF center was defined as the centroid of the region defined by the contour (using MATLAB function centroid).
evidence: This describes the method for defining receptive field centers.

claim: Orientation tuning data were obtained using luminance contrast edges with 12 orientations, 2 contrast polarities, 54% luminance contrast, and 200 ms stimulus duration.
source: A data set for orientation tuning was obtained using luminance contrast edges similar to those used for RF mapping, but with a circular window, sized and positioned such that the stimulus covered and was centered on the estimated aggregate cRF of the probe (12 orientations; 2 contrast polarities; 54 % luminance contrast; 200 ms stimulus duration).
evidence: This describes the stimuli used for orientation tuning measurements.

claim: Border ownership stimuli consisted of an isoluminant square positioned on an isoluminant background.
source: An isoluminant square was positioned on an isoluminant background, as in prior studies on border ownership (Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the border ownership stimuli.

claim: There were four basic border ownership conditions consisting of a factorial combination of two square positions and two contrast polarities.
source: There were four basic conditions (Figure 1A and C), consisting of a factorial combination of two square positions and two contrast polarities.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for border ownership testing.

claim: Luminance contrast in border ownership stimuli was 54%.
source: The two luminance areas in each scene were either both grays or a combination of gray and a color, and luminance contrast was 54%, as in prior studies (Zhou et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes a parameter of the border ownership stimuli.

claim: Square sizes in border ownership stimuli were between 12 × 12 and 20 × 20 dva.
source: Square sizes were between 12 × 12 and 20 × 20 dva.
evidence: This describes the size range of border ownership stimuli.

claim: After the animal maintained fixation for 400 ms, the border ownership stimulus appeared for 500 ms.
source: After the animal maintained fixation for 400 ms, the border ownership stimulus appeared for 500 ms.
evidence: This describes the temporal structure of trials.

claim: Typically 8-10 repetitions were obtained per condition.
source: Typically 8–10 repetitions were obtained per condition.
evidence: This describes the number of trial repetitions.

claim: The data were sorted offline using SpyKING CIRCUS.
source: The data were sorted offline using SpyKING CIRCUS (Yger et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting method.

claim: Well-isolated units were identified based on a well-defined refractory period in the interspike-interval histogram.
source: Well-isolated units were identified based on a well-defined refractory period in the interspike-interval histogram.
evidence: This describes the criterion for identifying well-isolated units.

claim: Multiunit clusters had to pass a signal-to-noise ratio criterion: peak-to-peak amplitude of the average waveform had to exceed five times the standard deviation of the signal 5 ms prior to the peak.
source: Multiunit clusters included in the analysis had to pass a criterion for the signal-to-noise ratio: peak-to-peak amplitude of the average waveform had to exceed five times the standard deviation of the signal 5 ms prior to the peak (similar to Kashkoush et al., 2019), after high-pass filtering the data (1-pole butterworth filter, cutoff 300 Hz, implemented using functions butter and filtfilt in MATLAB).
evidence: This describes the quality criterion for multiunit clusters.

claim: Spikes were counted in a window [30 100] ms after each stimulus onset for receptive field mapping.
source: To determine the cRF, spikes were counted in a window [30 100] ms after each stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes the analysis window for receptive field mapping.

claim: The outline of the cRF was defined as the contour at z = 3 on the smoothed spatial map.
source: The outline of the cRF was defined as the contour at z = 3 on this smoothed map (calculated using MATLAB function contourc).
evidence: This describes the method for defining receptive field boundaries.

claim: A unit's response was evaluated for border ownership selectivity if it passed five inclusion criteria.
source: A unit's response was evaluated for border ownership selectivity if it passed the following inclusion criteria: (1) average spike rate was ≥1 spike/s for at least one of the four conditions; (2) the evoked spike count for at least one of the four conditions was significantly different from that recorded prior to all trials across conditions (two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test [MATLAB function ranksum] with Bonferroni correction); (3) at least six trials per condition were available; (4) the central edge of the squares in the border ownership stimulus intersected the cRF; (5) the distance between any part of the cRF contour and any part of the noncentral edges of the squares in the border ownership stimulus was ≥1 dva.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for border ownership analysis.

claim: Statistical significance of border ownership selectivity was evaluated using a permutation test with 10,000 shuffles.
source: Statistical significance of border ownership selectivity was evaluated using a permutation test: a null distribution was created by shuffling the border ownership stimulus labels 10,000 times, separately for each luminance contrast pair, and the p value was estimated as the fraction of |BOIshuffled| that was at least as large as |BOI|.
evidence: This describes the statistical test for border ownership selectivity.

claim: A data set was defined to be border ownership-selective if p < 0.05 with Bonferroni correction if multiple orientations or positions were available.
source: A data set was defined to be border ownership-selective if p < 0.05 (with Bonferroni correction if multiple orientations or positions were available for the same unit)
evidence: This describes the criterion for border ownership selectivity.

claim: Spike trains were rounded to 0.1 ms resolution and convolved with a postsynaptic kernel for time course analysis.
source: Spike trains were rounded to 0.1 ms resolution and convolved with a postsynaptic kernel K(t) (Thompson et al., 1996)
evidence: This describes the method for computing response time courses.

claim: The postsynaptic kernel used had parameters τg = 1 ms and τd = 20 ms.
source: where τg = 1 ms and τd = 20 ms.
evidence: This describes the parameters of the postsynaptic kernel.

claim: Confidence intervals (95%) on latencies were calculated using a bootstrap approach with the bias corrected and accelerated percentile method with 2000 bootstraps.
source: Confidence intervals (95%) were calculated on these latencies using a bootstrap approach with the bias corrected and accelerated percentile method (MATLAB function bootci, 2000 bootstraps).
evidence: This describes the method for computing confidence intervals.

claim: Border ownership reliability (BOR) was computed in 100 ms sliding windows with 1 ms steps.
source: This metric was computed for the border ownership-selective units in each laminar compartment, in 100 ms sliding windows (1 ms steps).
evidence: This describes the temporal parameters for BOR analysis.

claim: For each unit, 10,000 sets of four spike trains were generated for BOR calculation.
source: For each unit, 10,000 sets of four spike trains were generated, where each set contained one random spike train from each of the four conditions in Figure 1A and C.
evidence: This describes the resampling procedure for BOR calculation.

claim: For every window position, BOR was only computed if there were at least 10 spikes across conditions.
source: For each window position for each unit, BOR was only computed if there were at least 10 spikes across conditions.
evidence: This describes a criterion for BOR calculation.

claim: The proportion of units sharing the most common preferred side of border ownership was compared with a null distribution generated by randomly assigning the preferred side (2000 randomizations).
source: The proportion of units sharing the most common preferred side was calculated for each penetration. The average of these proportions across penetrations (Ppref) was compared with a null distribution generated by randomly assigning the preferred side of border ownership for each data set (2000 randomizations; that is, a binomial process with chance of success = 0.5).
evidence: This describes the statistical test for clustering of border ownership preference.

claim: Orientation selectivity was evaluated using a Kruskal-Wallis test on evoked spike counts with orientation as the grouping variable, with significance defined as p < 0.05.
source: Orientation selectivity was evaluated using a Kruskal–Wallis test (MATLAB function kruskalwallis) on the evoked spike counts in the analysis window (between 30 ms and 200 after stimulus onset) from the orientation tuning data set, using orientation as the grouping variable (Pettine et al., 2019), and defined as p < 0.05.
evidence: This describes the statistical test for orientation selectivity.

claim: All units for which the center of the contrast edge was positioned in the cRF and the z-scored spike rate for the orientation with the highest rate was ≥3 were included in orientation analysis.
source: All units for which the center of the contrast edge in the orientation data set was positioned in the cRF, and the z-scored spike rate for the orientation with the highest rate was ≥3 were included.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for orientation analysis.

claim: The independence between the fractions of orientation-selective and border ownership-selective units was assessed using a Chi-square test.
source: The independence between the fractions of, respectively, orientation-selective and border ownership-selective units (Table 1) was assessed using a Chi-square test (MATLAB function crosstab).
evidence: This describes the statistical test for independence between selectivity types.

claim: The shortest distance of data points to the identity line was analyzed by comparing the mean to a null distribution generated by shuffling values (2000 shuffles).
source: The shortest distance of the data points in Figure 6C to the identity line (Figure 6D) was analyzed by comparing the mean to a null distribution generated by shuffling the values for the preferred edge orientation and the circular mean of border ownership-selective orientations, and calculating the mean of the shortest distance to the identity line (2000 shuffles).
evidence: This describes the statistical test for the relationship between orientation and border ownership preferences.
